questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A patient with a traumatic lesion of the left half of the spinal cord at the level of the eighth cervical segment might present the following sign(s) and symptom(s):
questions.explanation: In left hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome), the corticospinal tract is damaged on the left side, causing ipsilateral UMN signs below the lesion. Option D is correct because the left corticospinal damage produces left-sided positive Babinski sign below C8. Option A is wrong (pain/temp loss is contralateral in spinothalamic tract damage). Option B is wrong (position sense loss is ipsilateral in dorsal column damage). Option C is wrong (hemiplegia would be ipsilateral, not right). Option E is wrong (LMN signs occur at the lesion level, not below).
questions.keyConcept: In spinal cord hemisection, ipsilateral UMN paralysis and Babinski sign occur below the lesion due to corticospinal tract damage.
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensations on the left side below the level of the lesion
Loss of position sense of the right leg
Right-sided lower motor paralysis in the segment of the lesion and muscular atrophy

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: 24-year-old man was brought to the ER following a driving accident. Neurological testing revealed paraplegia and loss of all sensory modalities in bilateral lower limbs. Sensation for the upper limbs and the trunk was intact. Which of the following might be the nature and location of the lesion in this patient?
questions.explanation: The presentation of bilateral lower limb paralysis with intact upper limbs and trunk suggests central cord syndrome. Option C is correct because complete transection at T8 would paralyze everything below T8 (including trunk). Option E (central cord syndrome) is typically at C5-C6 levels and affects upper limbs more than lower due to the somatotopic arrangement of the corticospinal tract. The patient has paraplegia with intact upper limbs, which is most consistent with a T8 cord lesion where the corticospinal fibers for lower limbs are most affected.
questions.keyConcept: Central cord syndrome preferentially affects upper extremities due to the somatotopic organization of corticospinal fibers in the spinal cord.
options: Complete section of spinal cord at C8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at C8 level
Complete section of spinal cord at T8 level
Hemi section of spinal cord at T8 level

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 42-year-old right-handed male arrives to the emergency department and is intoxicated. At the time of presentation, he is unable to move his hands and arms. The following day, once he is sober, a more thorough neurological examination reveals a complete flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs and severely diminished-to-absent reflex activity. What is the most likely area of spinal damage?
questions.explanation: This question appears to reference a spinal cord cross-section image showing different horn regions. Area C corresponds to the anterior horn where lower motor neurons reside. Damage to anterior horn cells at C8 level (or nearby) causes flaccid paralysis of the upper limbs with areflexia due to LMN destruction. This is consistent with anterior cord syndrome from watershed infarction, commonly seen after cardiac arrest or severe hypotension. The flaccid paralysis and absent reflexes indicate LMN, not UMN lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior horn cell damage causes flaccid paralysis with areflexia due to destruction of lower motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Crude touch sensation is:
questions.explanation: Crude touch is carried by Aδ fibers (lightly myelinated, 2-5 μm diameter, 5-15 m/s conduction). Option A is correct. Option B is wrong (crude touch is poorly localized, fine touch is sharply localized). Option C is wrong (crude touch is carried in anterior spinothalamic tract, not lateral). Option D is wrong (perceived at thalamic level, not cortex). Option E is wrong (receptors for crude touch are phasic, not tonic).
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch uses Aδ fibers and is carried in the anterior spinothalamic tract with poor localization.
options: Carried in the lateral spinothalamic tract.
Perceived at level of sensory cortex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In the nigrostriated lesion there is:
questions.explanation: Nigrostriatal lesions (Parkinson's disease) cause lead-pipe rigidity, not spasticity or kinetic tremors. Option B is correct. Lead-pipe rigidity is a hallmark of Parkinsonian rigidity - constant resistance throughout range of motion. Option A is wrong (kinetic tremors are cerebellar). Option C is wrong (positive Babinski is UMN sign, not typical of basal ganglia lesions). Option D is wrong (rebound phenomenon is cerebellar). Option E is wrong (spasticity is corticospinal, not basal ganglia).
questions.keyConcept: Nigrostriatal lesions cause lead-pipe rigidity with constant resistance throughout passive range of motion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A patient suffering from damage of basal ganglia may NOT show:
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia lesions do NOT cause hyperreflexia and clonus - these are UMN signs. Option B is correct. The basal ganglia lesions cause hypokinetic movements (hypokinesia), shuffling gait, and tremor, but not hyperreflexia. Option A is wrong (static tremors occur in basal ganglia lesions). Option C is wrong (shuffling gait is a feature). Option D is wrong (degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra is the cause of Parkinson's). Option E is wrong (hypokinesia does occur).
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia lesions cause hypokinetic features (hypokinesia, shuffling gait) with normal or decreased reflexes, not hyperreflexia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Basal ganglia lesion may Not cause:
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia lesions cause rigidity, not flaccidity. Option E is correct. Flaccidity is a LMN sign or occurs with cerebellar lesions. Parkinsonian basal ganglia lesions produce cogwheel rigidity, not flaccidity. Options A-D are all recognized features of basal ganglia dysfunction: akinesia (inability to initiate movement), mask face (hypomimia), cogwheel rigidity, and monotonous speech.
questions.keyConcept: Basal ganglia lesions produce extrapyramidal signs including rigidity and akinesia, not flaccidity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson's disease:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is caused by lesion in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Option A is correct. The substantia nigra produces dopamine; its degeneration leads to dopamine deficiency in the striatum, causing Parkinsonian symptoms. Option B is wrong (thalamic lesions cause sensory symptoms, not Parkinsonism). Option C is wrong (Parkinsonism has resting tremors, not kinetic). Option D is wrong (clasp-knife rigidity is UMN, not Parkinsonian). Option E is wrong (pendular jerks are cerebellar).
questions.keyConcept: Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
options: Is caused by a lesion in the substantia nigra.
Is caused by lesion in the posteroventral nucleus of the thalamus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Parkinsonism:
questions.explanation: Clasp-knife spasticity is a pyramidal/UMN feature, NOT Parkinsonism. Option C is correct. Parkinsonian rigidity is lead-pipe or cogwheel type, not clasp-knife. Options A, B, D, E are all features of Parkinsonism: resting tremor, dopamine deficiency, difficulty initiating movements, and preserved reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian rigidity is lead-pipe or cogwheel type, distinct from the clasp-knife spasticity of pyramidal lesions.
options: A deficiency of dopamine in the substantia nigra.
A clasp-knife type of spastic rigidity.
Difficulty in initiating the voluntary movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson's disease is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by lead-pipe rigidity. Option D is correct. The resting tremor worsens with action (not at rest as stated in option A). Paralysis is not a feature (option B is wrong). Dopamine is decreased, not increased (option C is wrong). Clonus is not a Parkinsonian feature (option E is wrong). Lead-pipe rigidity with cogwheel phenomenon is pathognomonic.
questions.keyConcept: Lead-pipe rigidity is the characteristic motor sign of Parkinson's disease, with constant resistance throughout passive movement.
options: Paralysis of one side of the body.
Increase of dopamine in the substantia nigra.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Chorea:
questions.explanation: Chorea is associated with hypotonia. Option C is correct. Chorea results from basal ganglia (caudate/putamen) lesions causing involuntary, irregular movements with reduced tone. Option A is wrong (substantia nigra lesions cause Parkinsonism, not chorea). Option B is wrong (internal capsule lesions cause UMN signs). Option D is wrong (exaggerated tendon jerk occurs in UMN lesions, not chorea). Option E is wrong (increased gamma activity causes hypertonia, opposite of chorea).
questions.keyConcept: Chorea presents with irregular, involuntary movements and hypotonia due to basal ganglia dysfunction.
options: Is due to lesion in the substantia nigra.
May be due to lesion in the internal capsule.
Is associated with exaggerated tendon jerk.
Is associated with increased gamma activity

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Athetosis is associated with movement which is NOT:
questions.explanation: Athetosis movements are NOT decreased by emotions - they increase with emotional states. Option E is correct. Athetosis consists of slow, twisting, spontaneous movements that intensify with emotional stress, fatigue, and attempts at voluntary movement. Option A, B, C, D all correctly describe athetoid movements.
questions.keyConcept: Athetoid movements intensify with emotional states and voluntary attempts, distinguishing them from other movement disorders.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning the basal ganglia function, which is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Basal ganglia mainly regulate/inhibit movement, not increase muscle tone. Option D is correct. The basal ganglia work through indirect pathways to inhibit excessive movement and regulate motor planning. Increased muscle tone is a brainstem/spinal cord function. Options A, B, C, and E all accurately describe basal ganglia functions in movement planning, timing, and suppression of unwanted movements.
questions.keyConcept: The basal ganglia modulate movement patterns and timing while suppressing involuntary movements, rather than directly increasing muscle tone.
options: Caudate nucleus plan the sequence of patterns of movement.
Caudate nucleus modifies the timing of movements.
Putamen helps execution of subconscious learned pattern of movement.
Basal ganglia mainly increases the muscle tone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The neurotransmitter used by the axons of substantia nigra neurons which project to the caudate and putamen is :
questions.explanation: The neurotransmitter used by substantia nigra neurons projecting to caudate and putamen is dopamine. Option C is correct. These neurons form the nigrostriatal pathway. When they degenerate (as in Parkinson's), dopamine levels in the striatum drop, causing motor symptoms. Option A is wrong (ACh is used locally in striatum). Options B, D, E are wrong neurotransmitters for this pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine is the nigrostriatal neurotransmitter; its deficiency causes Parkinson's disease motor symptoms.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the cerebellum, which is NOT true:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum has INDIRECT stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons via the red nucleus and thalamus, not direct. Option D is incorrect. Options A, B, C, E are all true: cerebellum helps plan and time movements, receives input from motor cortex, receives spindle/GTO input via spinocerebellar tracts, and predicts successive movements.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar influence on motor neurons is indirect, acting through the red nucleus and thalamus to modulate cortical output.
options: Cerebellum helps in planning and timing of voluntary movements.
The cerebellum is stimulated by the motor cortex.
The receptor activity of the spindles and Golgi tendons organs reaches the cerebellum through the spinocerebellar tract.
The cerebellum has direct stimulatory effect on alpha motor neurons.
The cerebellum predicts and plans for the successive movements

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The cerebellum is NOT involved in:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellum INCREASES muscle tone, not decreases. Option E is incorrect. Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia. Options A-D are all true: cerebellum maintains posture, provides continuous feedback, coordinates rapid alternating movements, and the neocerebellum increases (not decreases) muscle tone.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum facilitates muscle tone; lesions cause hypotonia and movement incoordination.
options: Continuous feedback of information even during action.
The performance of rapid alternating movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which one of the following is NOT true regarding the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar ataxia is sensory ataxia - it worsens with eye closure (positive Romberg). Option B is INCORRECT as stated. Actually, cerebellar ataxia is NOT sensory (sensory ataxia is dorsal column dysfunction). The correct answer is B because cerebellar ataxia is motor ataxia, characterized by clumsiness that is visible with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which hides behind visual compensation. Wait - re-reading: cerebellar ataxia is a motor (not sensory) ataxia that DOES NOT require visual compensation to demonstrate.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is a motor coordination deficit visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which requires eye closure to manifest.
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere controls movements of the ipsilateral muscles.
Cerebellar ataxia is a sensory ataxia.
Cerebellar lesions cause pendular knee jerks.
The intention tremor associated with cerebellar disease is worsened by movement.
The neocerebellar syndrome gait is zig-zag like.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellum helps planning of movements. Option D is correct. The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) receives input from motor and premotor cortex and helps in movement planning and timing. Option A is wrong (each hemisphere controls ipsilateral muscles). Option B is wrong (spinocerebellar tracts provide unconscious proprioception). Option C is wrong (paleocerebellum调节肌张力). Option E is wrong (cerebellar ataxia has hypotonia, not spasticity).
questions.keyConcept: The neocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) is crucial for movement planning and coordination with the motor cortex.
options: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the contralateral muscles.
Spinocerebellar tracts give rise to conscious recognition of joint position sense.
Paleocerbellar is facilitatory to muscle tone.
Cerebellar ataxia is associated with spasticity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which is NOT a function of the cerebellum includes:
questions.explanation: The cerebellum INHIBITS excess cortical activity, not inhibits cortical activity per se (which would be incorrect). Option E is poorly worded. Actually, the cerebellum projects to thalamus and cerebral cortex via the dentatothalamic pathway, modulating (facilitating or inhibiting) cortical motor areas. This helps fine-tune movements. The cerebellum doesn't directly inhibit cortical output but regulates it.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum modulates cortical motor output through the dentatothalamic pathway, regulating movement precision.
options: Stop the movement at the precise intended point.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Neocerebellar syndrome in humans is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellar syndrome is NOT characterized by static tremors - these are Parkinsonian. Option E is correct. Neocerebellar syndrome features include hypotonia, pendular knee jerks, ataxia, dysarthria, and intention tremor (not static). Static tremors are characteristic of Parkinson's disease due to basal ganglia dysfunction.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellar syndrome features intention tremor (worse with movement), not the resting/static tremor of Parkinsonism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Adiadochokinesia:
questions.explanation: Adiadochokinesia is failure to perform rapid alternating movements. Option A is correct. This is a classic cerebellar sign. It is due to lesion in the cerebellum (especially neocerebellum). Options B, C, D are wrong (caudate, subthalamus, vestibulocerebellum lesions cause different symptoms). Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia, not hypertonia (option E is wrong).
questions.keyConcept: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements (dysdiadochokinesia) indicates cerebellar dysfunction.
options: Is failure of the patient to perform rapid coordinate movements.
Is due to lesion in caudate nucleus.
Is due to lesion in subthalamus.
Is due to lesion in vestibulocerebellum.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The following is NOT a neurological feature of cerebellar lesion:
questions.explanation: Shuffling gait is NOT a cerebellar feature - it is a Parkinsonian gait. Option D is correct. Cerebellar lesions cause ataxic gait (wide-based, staggering), not shuffling gait. Options A, B, C, E are all cerebellar signs: abnormal coordination, rebound phenomenon, dysdiadochokinesia, and kinetic tremors.
questions.keyConcept: Shuffling gait is characteristic of basal ganglia disease (Parkinsonism), not cerebellar lesions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which sentence is NOT true about kinetic tremors:
questions.explanation: Kinetic tremors occur during MOVEMENT, not at rest. Option A is INCORRECT and therefore the correct answer. Kinetic/intention tremors worsen with voluntary movement and are cerebellar. Option B, C, D, E all correctly describe kinetic tremors as neocerebellar, accompanied by hypotonia, disappearing during sleep, and associated with motor ataxia.
questions.keyConcept: Kinetic tremor is a movement-dependent tremor of cerebellar origin, unlike the resting tremor of Parkinsonism.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Neocerebellum syndrome is NOT associated with:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellum syndrome is NOT associated with hypertonia - it causes hypotonia. Option B is correct. Cerebellar lesions characteristically reduce muscle tone. Options A, C, D, E are all associated with neocerebellar syndrome: ataxia, inability to perform complex movements, rebound phenomenon, and decomposition of movements.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia due to loss of cerebellar facilitatory influence on muscle tone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Neocerebellum disease is associated with:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellum disease is associated with zigzag gait. Option B is correct. The neocerebellum controls coordination of voluntary movements; lesions cause ataxic gait that is wide-based and staggering (drunken/zigzag). Option A (shuffling) is Parkinsonian. Option C (stamping) is sensory ataxia. Option D (circumduction) is UMN gait. Option E (drunken gait) is actually correct but zigzag is more specific for neocerebellar lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Neocerebellar lesions produce a characteristic zigzag or drunken ataxic gait due to loss of movement coordination.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A cerebellar lesion is most likely associated with severe loss of equilibrium and drunken gait when the lesion involves:
questions.explanation: Lesion of the flocculonodular lobe causes severe equilibrium loss and drunken gait. Option D is correct. The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) receives vestibular input and controls balance. Lesions cause severe ataxia, especially of trunk and gait, with patients being unable to stand without support. The neocerebellum affects appendicular coordination, not truncal equilibrium primarily.
questions.keyConcept: The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe) is essential for truncal stability and equilibrium.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The following is NOT a neurological feature of cerebellar lesion:
questions.explanation: Lead-pipe rigidity is NOT a cerebellar feature - it is Parkinsonian. Option B is correct. Cerebellar lesions cause hypotonia, not rigidity. Options A, C, D, E are all cerebellar signs: dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, rebound phenomenon, and incoordination.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar signs include hypotonia, dysmetria, and coordination deficits, not rigidity.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Spasticity is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Spasticity is of clasp-knife nature. Option E is correct. Clasp-knife spasticity is velocity-dependent increased tone with sudden release, characteristic of UMN lesions. Options A, B, C, D are incorrect: spasticity affects antigravity muscles primarily; is due to UMN (not basal ganglia) lesions; is associated with static/resting tremors (Parkinsonian); and clonus is not defining characteristic.
questions.keyConcept: Clasp-knife spasticity is the hallmark of corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesions, with sudden release after initial resistance.
options: Due to increase alpha and gamma cells activities.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Rigidity is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Rigidity is characterized by increased tone in antigravity muscles. Option A is correct. Rigidity (both lead-pipe and cogwheel) particularly affects anti-gravity muscles due to exaggerated extensor activity. Options B, C, D, E are incorrect: gamma cell hyperactivity alone doesn't cause rigidity; rigidity occurs in UMN lesions (not just associated); static tremors are Parkinsonian; circumduction gait is UMN, not rigidity.
questions.keyConcept: Rigidity preferentially affects antigravity muscles, reflecting the dominance of extensor muscles in human posture.
options: Due to increase gamma cells activities.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Spasticity is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Spasticity is associated with clonus. Option D is correct. Clonus (rhythmic oscillatory movements) is a feature of spastic UMN lesions. Options A, B, C, E are incorrect: shuffling gait is Parkinsonian; normoreflexia is normal; cogwheel/lead-pipe is rigidity not spasticity; clonus does NOT occur in Parkinsonism (which has resting tremor, not clonus).
questions.keyConcept: Clonus is a hallmark of spastic UMN lesions, presenting as rhythmic, involuntary muscular contractions.
options: Is of Cog-wheel or lead pipe nature.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Motor ataxia is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is characterized by FAILURE of coordination even with opened eyes. Option D is INCORRECT. Motor (cerebellar) ataxia shows poor coordination visible even with eyes open, unlike sensory ataxia which compensates with vision. Options A, B, C, E are correct features of motor ataxia: zigzag gait, staccato speech, kinetic tremors, and cerebellar origin.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar ataxia is manifest with eyes open due to loss of motor coordination, unlike sensory ataxia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Sensory ataxia is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Sensory ataxia is characterized by stamping gait. Option A is correct. Sensory ataxia results from dorsal column dysfunction causing loss of proprioception; patients stamp their feet hard to gain vibratory and position sense feedback. Options B, C, D, E describe cerebellar features: staccato speech, kinetic tremors, failure of coordination with eyes open, and cerebellar lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory ataxia presents with stamping gait as patients rely on heavy foot contact to compensate for lost proprioception.
options: Failure of coordination even with opened eyes

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is true with respect to the corticospinal pathway:
questions.explanation: The corticospinal pathway is a multineuron pathway. Option D is correct. The corticospinal tract has upper motor neurons in motor cortex that synapse with lower motor neurons in the spinal cord (via interneurons or directly). Option A is wrong (intact tract = negative Babinski). Option B is wrong (synapses with LMN in cord). Option C is wrong (it is contralateral, not ipsilateral, in the spinal cord after decussation at pyramids).
questions.keyConcept: The corticospinal pathway is a multineuronal system with upper and lower motor neurons connected via interneurons in the spinal cord.
options: It must be intact to elicit a positive Babinski's sign.
It synapses with gamma motor neurons in the spinal cord.
Is mostly an ipsilateral pathway in the spinal cord.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Purkinji cells of the cerebellar cortex are excited by:
questions.explanation: Purkinje cells are excited by granule cells. Option B is correct. Granule cells receive input from mossy fibers and then send parallel fibers to excite Purkinje cells. This is the main excitatory input to Purkinje cells in the cerebellar cortex. Option A is wrong (deep nuclei provide input to Purkinje cells via inhibition). Option C is wrong (basket cells inhibit Purkinje cells).
questions.keyConcept: Granule cells provide the primary excitatory input to Purkinje cells via parallel fibers in the cerebellar cortex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A major function of the climbing fibers to cerebellar cortex is:
questions.explanation: Climbing fiber function includes learning novel movement patterns. Option B is correct. Climbing fibers carry error signals and teach the cerebellum about unexpected events, contributing to motor learning ( cerebellar long-term depression). Option A is wrong (climbing fibers excite Purkinje cells, not inhibit). Option C is wrong (emotional stimuli are limbic, not cerebellar climbing fiber function). Option D is wrong (Purkinje cells, not climbing fibers, directly influence motor neurons via deep nuclei).
questions.keyConcept: Climbing fibers convey error signals to the cerebellum for motor learning and adaptation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 65 year-old man has been complaining of worsening tremors at rest and difficulty in walking. On examination he is expected to reveal:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease has normal tendon jerks (normoreflexia). Option C is correct. Parkinsonian patients have normal reflexes because the reflex arc itself is intact; the pathology is in the basal ganglia, not in the motor neurons or reflex pathways. Options A, B, D are incorrect: flaccidity is LMN, frequent micturition is not typical, and lost superficial reflexes occur in UMN lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinson's disease preserves normal reflexes because the reflex arc remains intact despite basal ganglia degeneration.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Pre-motor cortex:
questions.explanation: Pre-motor cortex controls movements like speech, eye and head movements. Option B is correct. The premotor area (area 6) is rostral to motor cortex and programs movements, especially those involving proximal muscles and axial/girdle muscles. Option A is wrong (premotor is in frontal lobe, not temporal). Option C is wrong (facilitates stretch reflex is area 4). Option D is wrong (fine skilled movements are area 4).
questions.keyConcept: Premotor cortex (area 6) programs complex movements involving speech, eye, and head coordination.
options: Is found in the temporal cortex.
Control movements as speech, eye and head movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The motor area 4 is:
questions.explanation: Motor area 4 is the main cortical area responsible for control of fine discrete movements. Option D is correct. Primary motor cortex (area 4) in the precentral gyrus is the main origin of corticospinal tract. Option A is wrong (area 4 is precentral, not postcentral). Option B is wrong (area 4 facilitates tone, not inhibits). Option C is wrong (pyramidal tract originates from area 4).
questions.keyConcept: Primary motor cortex (area 4) in the precentral gyrus is the key area for fine, discrete voluntary movements.
options: Located in the post central gyrus in the frontal lobe.
Main site of origin of extrapyranidal tract.
The main cortical area responsible for control of fine discrete movements

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: lesion of motor area 6 causes:
questions.explanation: Lesion of motor area 6 causes increased muscle tone. Option A is correct. Premotor area 6 has connections with basal ganglia and brainstem motor areas; lesions cause release of extensor tone (rigidity). Option B is wrong (paralysis is area 4 lesion). Option C is wrong (loss of fine movements is area 4). Option D is wrong (positive Babinski with dorsiflexion is corticospinal). Option E is wrong (inhibition of grasp reflex is not expected).
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area 6 lesions release extensor muscle tone due to loss of indirect pathway modulation.
options: Positive Babeniski’s sign with dorsiflexion of the big toe.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The extrapyramidal system:
questions.explanation: The extrapyramidal system is inhibitory to muscle tone. Option E is correct. The extrapyramidal system (basal ganglia, red nucleus, reticular formation) normally inhibits muscle tone. When damaged, rigidity results. Option A is wrong (originates from cortex AND brainstem). Option B is wrong (not 90% crossed). Option C is wrong (terminates at gamma neurons, not alpha). Option D is wrong (active from birth).
questions.keyConcept: Extrapyramidal system normally inhibits muscle tone; lesions result in rigidity.
options: About 90% of its descending fibers are crossed to the opposite side.
Terminates at alpha & gamma neurons in the sp. cord & the cranial nuclei.
Starts its function during the first year of life.
Is inhibitory to the muscle tone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Neocerebellar lesions are associated with:
questions.explanation: Neocerebellar lesions are associated with pendular knee jerk. Option D is correct. The cerebellum facilitates stretch reflex; when damaged, the reflex becomes unopposed and pendular (oscillates). Options A, B, C are incorrect: clasp-knife rigidity is UMN, positive Romberg is sensory ataxia, monotonous speech is from basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: Pendular knee jerks indicate cerebellar hypotonus due to loss of cerebellar modulation of stretch reflex.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the cerebellum, all the following are true except:
questions.explanation: Cerebellum CAN initiate gross movements (Option B is INCORRECT). The cerebellum coordinates but does not initiate movements; the cerebrum initiates. Options A, C, D are true: cerebellum has reverberating circuits (via deep nuclei), prevents overshooting, and acts as a programmer for movements. The cerebellum fine-tunes motor commands but the cerebral cortex initiates voluntary movements.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum coordinates and refines motor commands but does not initiate voluntary movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson’s disease is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by increased activity of alpha motor neurons. Option D is incorrect but seems to be the intended answer. Actually, Parkinson's has decreased alpha activity due to rigidity... Wait re-reading: Option D says 'increased activity of α motor neurons' - this is wrong. Parkinson's involves loss of dopamine → increased inhibitory output from basal ganglia → decreased thalamic facilitation → actually DECREASED alpha activity. But the question may be interpreted differently. Let me reconsider: Option A (decreased dopamine in GP) is true for Parkinsonism. The question asks what Parkinson's is NOT characterized by - Option D is incorrect.
questions.keyConcept: Parkinson's disease involves loss of dopaminergic neurons and decreased thalamic facilitation of cortical motor areas.
options: Decreased dopamine in the globus pallidus.
Increased activity of α motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compared to static tremors, intention tremors:
questions.explanation: Intention tremors are caused by loss of damping function of cerebellum. Option C is correct. Intention (kinetic) tremor occurs when the cerebellum fails to dampen movements, worsening as target is approached. Options A, B, D describe static/rest tremors and basal ganglia: resting tremors occur in Parkinsonism, accompanied by hypertonia, and are characteristic of basal ganglia lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Intention tremor reflects cerebellar dysfunction in movement dampening and coordination feedback.
options: Are caused by loss of damping function of cerebellum.
Are characteristic to basal ganglia lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning the basal ganglia function:
questions.explanation: Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements. Option D is correct. The caudate circuit (caudate-putamen-GP-SNr-thalamus-caudate) is involved in movement scaling and timing. Option A is wrong (putamen executes learned patterns). Option B is wrong (caudate circuit is cognitive, putamen is motor). Option C is wrong (caudate circuit terminates in premotor, not motor area 4).
questions.keyConcept: Caudate nucleus circuits process movement scaling and timing through cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic loops.
options: Caudate circuit helps execution of learned pattern of movement.
Putamen circuit is important for cognitive control of voluntary movements.
Caudate circuit terminates in motor area 4.
Damage to caudate circuit results in loss of timing and scaling of movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Rigidity of parkinsonism:
questions.explanation: Rigidity in Parkinsonism occurs in agonist and antagonist muscles. Option C is correct. Parkinsonian rigidity affects both agonist and antagonist muscles equally throughout movement range. Option A is wrong (Parkinsonian rigidity differs from UMNL spasticity). Option B is wrong (prominence in antigravity muscles is UMN). Option D is wrong (gamma activity contributes but not the main cause).
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian rigidity equally affects agonist and antagonist muscles, unlike spasticity which predominates in antigravity muscles.
options: Is similar to that of UMNL.
Is more prominent in antigravity muscles.
Occurs in agonist and antagonist muscles.
Is mainly due to increased activity of gamma motor neurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson,s disease causes:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease causes increased resistance throughout range of movement. Option B is correct. Lead-pipe rigidity is constant resistance throughout passive movement range. Options A, C, D are wrong: no paralysis in Parkinsonism; decreased (not increased) facial movements; tremors are at rest (not during movements).
questions.keyConcept: Parkinsonian lead-pipe rigidity shows constant resistance throughout the full range of passive movement.
options: Increased resistance throughout the range of movement.
Tremors, which are obvious during movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Concerning the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesion is associated with dysmetria. Option B is correct. Dysmetria (overshooting/undershooting target) is a cardinal cerebellar sign. Option A is wrong (lateral zone is for coordination, not servo-comparator which is intermediate). Option C is wrong (Purkinje cells are inhibitory to deep nuclei). Option D is wrong (mossy fibers are for established patterns, climbing fibers for learning).
questions.keyConcept: Dysmetria - inability to accurately reach a target - is a hallmark of cerebellar lesions.
options: The lateral zone has servo-comparator function.
Cerebellar lesion is associated with dysmetria.
The cerebellar output fibers originate from Purkinje cells.
Mossy fibers are involved in newly learned patterns of movements.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lesion in the left cerebellar hemisphere results in:
questions.explanation: Lesion in left cerebellar hemisphere results in falling to the left side. Option D is correct. Each cerebellar hemisphere controls ipsilateral muscles and balance. Option A is wrong (cerebellar lesions don't cause paralysis). Option B is wrong (tremors are ipsilateral). Option C is wrong (monotonous speech is basal ganglia).
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral ataxia and falling due to loss of coordinated muscle control.
options: Paralysis of voluntary movements on left side of the body.
Tremors on right side of the body.
Falling to the left side during walking.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Motor ataxia is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is characterized by kinetic tremor. Option D is correct. Cerebellar motor ataxia presents with kinetic tremor (worse during movement), not the stamping gait or positive Romberg of sensory ataxia. Options A, B describe sensory ataxia features. Option C (normal speech) is not characteristic - cerebellar patients have dysarthria.
questions.keyConcept: Kinetic tremor worsens with intentional movement and is characteristic of cerebellar motor ataxia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Dysdiadochokinesia is associated with lesions of the:
questions.explanation: Dysdiadochokinesia is associated with lesions of the cerebellum. Option C is correct. Inability to perform rapid alternating movements is a classic cerebellar sign. Options A, B, D are wrong (premotor, primary motor, basal ganglia lesions cause different symptoms).
questions.keyConcept: Dysdiadochokinesia (impaired rapid alternating movements) indicates cerebellar dysfunction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding servocomparator function of the cerebellum:
questions.explanation: Cerebellum compares intended plan with actual movement (servocomparator function). Option B is correct. The cerebellum receives copies of motor commands (efference copy) and actual movement feedback, comparing them to correct ongoing movements. Options A, C, D are wrong: cerebellum sends indirect (via thalamus) not direct messages; receives unconscious (not conscious) proprioception; receives plan from cortex not basal ganglia.
questions.keyConcept: The cerebellum acts as a servocomparator, matching intended movement with actual execution through continuous feedback.
options: Cerebellum sends direct corrective messages to muscles.
Cerebellum compares the intended plan of movement with the actual movement.
Cerebellum receives feedback information from muscles through conscious proprioceptive receptors.
Cerebellum receives a copy of plan of movement from basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: An 83-year-old man was referred to a medical centre with a history of difficulty in walking. During examination: he was unsteady on his feet, dysarthric, negative Romberg’s sign, and appearance of tremor during movement were observed. What is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: Motor ataxia is the most probable diagnosis. Option A is correct. The patient has unsteady gait, dysarthria, negative Romberg (intact proprioception), and tremor during movement - all cerebellar signs. Sensory ataxia (B) would have positive Romberg. Vestibular ataxia (C) would have vertigo/nystagmus. Hysterical ataxia (D) lacks consistency.
questions.keyConcept: Negative Romberg with movement tremor and dysarthria points to cerebellar (motor) ataxia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A musician has lost his ability to play the piano with no signs of muscle paralysis. What is the probable site of lesion?
questions.explanation: Lesion within premotor area (area 6) is most probable. Option D is correct. Piano playing requires coordinated, skilled movements programmed by premotor cortex, not primary motor cortex (which executes fine movements). Area 8 is frontal eye fields; areas 1,2,3 are somatosensory. Loss without paralysis suggests premotor rather than primary motor lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Premotor area (area 6) programs skilled sequential movements; lesions disrupt coordination without paralysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Spinal shock produces:-
questions.explanation: Spinal shock produces hypotension. Option B is correct. Loss of sympathetic outflow after spinal cord transection causes vasodilation and hypotension. Options A, C, D describe later effects (automatic micturition after shock, positive Babinski develops later, spasticity develops weeks later). During spinal shock: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, loss of bowel/bladder, hypotension.
questions.keyConcept: Acute spinal shock causes flaccid paralysis, areflexia, and hypotension due to loss of sympathetic tone.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Brown-Sequard syndrome is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of vibration sense on the same side below lesion. Option A is correct. Hemisection causes ipsilateral dorsal column loss (vibration, proprioception) and corticospinal loss (motor) below; contralateral spinothalamic loss (pain, temperature). Options B, C, D are incorrect (motor loss is ipsilateral, reflex loss at lesion level is LMN, pain loss is contralateral).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard hemisection produces ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.
options: Loss of vibration sense on the same side below level of the lesion
Loss of voluntary movements on the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of reflex movements on the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of pain sensation on the same side below the level of the lesion

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: 43 year old woman is evaluated in the hospital and is found to have multiple neurologic abnormalities from the level T 12 down. She has loss of vibration and proprioception on the left but these senses are present on the right side. She has absent pain and temperature sensation in the right side from T12 down. Motor power was lost in the left leg but normal motor strength in her right leg. What is the most likely cause of her neurologic symptoms?
questions.explanation: Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord. Option C is correct. Left hemisection explains: left vibration/proprioception loss (dorsal columns), right pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), left leg paralysis (corticospinal). Complete transection would affect both sides. Right hemisection would cause opposite findings.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral dorsal column and motor loss with contralateral spinothalamic loss indicates spinal cord hemisection on the side of motor/dorsal column deficits.
options: Complete spinal cord transection at upper thoracic segments.
Complete spinal cord transection at lower thoracic segments.
Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord
Hemisection on the right part of spinal cord

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: After falling down from a staircase, a young woman is found to have loss of voluntary movement on the right side of the body and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side below the mid thoracic region. The probable site of lesion is:
questions.explanation: Transection of the right half of spinal cord in upper thoracic region. Option A is correct. Right hemiplegia (right voluntary movement loss) and left pain/temperature loss indicate right Brown-Sequard syndrome. The motor fibers decussate at the cervicomedullary junction, so hemisection causes ipsilateral motor loss below the lesion.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral motor paralysis with contralateral pain/temperature loss indicates hemisection on the side of motor deficits.
options: Transection of the right half of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of the left side of the spinal cord in the upper thoracic region
Transection of sensory and motor pathways on the right side of the pons
Transection of the left half of the spinal cord in the lumbar region

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Upper motor neuron lesion shows the following except:
questions.explanation: UMNL shows spasticity, not flaccidity. Option C is incorrect (flaccidity is LMN). Options A, B, D are correct UMN signs: increased tone, positive Babinski, exaggerated deep reflexes. The UMN lesion releases lower motor neurons from cortical inhibition, causing hyperreflexia and spasticity.
questions.keyConcept: Upper motor neuron lesions cause spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia, not the flaccid paralysis of lower motor neuron lesions.
options: Increased muscle tone of affected muscles.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Lesion in the right internal capsule (UMNL) would result in:
questions.explanation: Internal capsule lesion causes contralateral (left) spastic paralysis. Option B is correct. Corticospinal fibers decussate in medulla; internal capsule damage affects fibers before decussation, causing contralateral UMN signs. Right internal capsule damage → left hemiplegia. Flaccidity (A) is LMN. Right-sided paralysis (C) is wrong. Babinski loss (D) is wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Internal capsule strokes cause contralateral spastic hemiplegia because corticospinal fibers have not yet decussated.
options: Flaccid paralysis on the right Side of body.
Spastic paralysis on the left Side of body.
Spastic paralysis on the right Side of body.
Loss of Babinski sign on both sides.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Patient with cerebellar lesion complains of the following except:
questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesions do NOT disturb autonomic functions. Option C is correct. Autonomic dysfunction is not a feature of cerebellar lesions. Options A, B, D are cerebellar features: dysarthria, ataxic gait, inability to adjust movements (dysmetria). Cerebellum is purely motor coordination, not autonomic control.
questions.keyConcept: Cerebellar lesions affect motor coordination (gait, speech, movement adjustment) but not autonomic functions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Parkinson’s disease is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Parkinson's disease is characterized by decreased dopamine in the basal ganglia. Option A is correct. Dopaminergic neuron loss in substantia nigra causes striatal dopamine deficiency. Options B, C, D are wrong: Parkinson's patients have difficulty initiating movements, no paralysis, and intention (kinetic) tremors are cerebellar not Parkinsonian.
questions.keyConcept: Dopamine deficiency in the striatum is the biochemical hallmark of Parkinson's disease.
options: Decreased dopamine in the basal ganglia.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Muscle tone:
questions.explanation: Muscle tone is decreased or lost in lower motor neuron lesion. Option C is correct. LMN destruction causes flaccid paralysis with hypotonia/areflexia because the efferent limb of the stretch reflex is gone. Options A, B, D are incorrect: tone is sustained (not rapidly fatiguing), based on static stretch reflex, and decreases during sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Lower motor neuron lesions eliminate muscle tone and stretch reflexes due to destruction of the efferent limb.
options: Is based on dynamic stretch reflex.
Is decreased Or lost in lower motor neuron lesion.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: When the sole is stroked firmly by a key:
questions.explanation: In UMNL, the other toes show fanning. Option D is correct. Positive Babinski (upgoing plantar response) in UMNL involves big toe extension and often toe fanning due to corticospinal release. Option A is wrong (plantar flexion = normal). Option B is wrong (Babinski is UMNL, not area 6 lesion). Option C is wrong (dorsiflexion in LMNL is not typical; LMNL causes absent plantar response).
questions.keyConcept: The Babinski sign (toe extension/fanning) indicates upper motor neuron lesion with corticospinal tract dysfunction.
options: The big toe planter-flexes in a patient having an UMNL.
The big toe dorsi-flexes in a patient with damaged area 6.
The big toe dorsi-flexes in a patient having LMNL.
The other toes show fanning in UMNL.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Mass reflex:
questions.explanation: Mass reflex has pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder. Option B is correct. Mass reflex is a spinal reflex appearing after spinal shock resolution in complete transection; strong stimuli to skin trigger flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge. Options A, C, D are incorrect (upper limb rigidity is wrong, immediate occurrence is wrong, basoganglia involvement is wrong).
questions.keyConcept: Mass reflex (flexor withdrawal with autonomic discharge) indicates complete spinal cord transection with recovered spinal reflexes.
options: Has a pattern of rigidity of upper limbs.
Has a pattern of massive lower limb flexion with emptying of rectum and bladder.
Occurs immediately after spinal cord transcetion.
Is elicited by in patients with basal ganglia lesions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Long-term effects of cord trans-section at T12 include:
questions.explanation: Long-term cord transection at T12: hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs. Option D is correct. After spinal shock resolves, UMN signs develop below the lesion (weeks to months). Options A, B, C are incorrect: bladder paralysis is not typical (autonomic dysreflexia occurs), tendon jerks are exaggerated (not lost), hyperalgesia is not typical.
questions.keyConcept: After spinal shock resolves, transection above T12 causes spastic paralysis with hyperreflexia in lower limbs.
options: Loss of tendon jerks in lower limbs.
Hypertonia and hyperreflexia in lower limbs.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit - this is NOT true. Option E is INCORRECT. Multiple alpha motor neurons innervate a single muscle; each alpha neuron with its fibers constitutes ONE motor unit, not all alpha cells. Option A is wrong (alpha are larger, not more numerous). Option B is true (supply extrafusal). Option C is true (lateral horn for fine movements). Option D is wrong (flexor alphas are rostral to extensor).
questions.keyConcept: Motor units are individual alpha motor neurons plus all muscle fibers they innervate; many motor units compose a single muscle.
options: They are larger and more numerous than gamma neurons.
They supply extrafusal skeletal muscle fibers.
Alpha in the lateral part of anterior horn are concerned with fine movements
Alpha of flexors are dorsally present to alpha of extensors
All alpha cells that supply a specific muscle represent the motor unit.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding alpha motor neurons, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Motor unit of distal limb muscle involves 200 fibers - this is NOT true. Option C is INCORRECT. Distal muscles (requiring fine control) have SMALL motor units (50-100 fibers per neuron), while proximal muscles have large units. The statement reverses this. Options A, B, D, E are true statements about alpha motor neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Distal muscles with fine control have small motor units (fewer fibers per neuron) for precision.
options: A single alpha cell + its axon + fibers innervated represent the motor unit.
Alpha is the final common pathway for muscle contraction.
The motor unit of distal limb muscle involves 200 fibers
Its discharge is affected by projections from higher centers.
Its discharge is affected by spinal cord interneurons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Compared to alpha motor neurons, gamma motor neurons are:
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons innervate the muscle spindle. Option D is correct. Gamma motor neurons supply intrafusal muscle fibers,调节 spindle sensitivity. Options A is wrong (alpha are more numerous). Option B is wrong (alpha supply extrafusal). Option C is wrong (two types exist). Option E is wrong (transmit from peripheral receptor).
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons regulate muscle spindle sensitivity by contracting intrafusal fibers during voluntary movement.
options: Supply ordinary contractile skeletal muscle fibers
Transmit impulses from the central part of intrafusal fibers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which statement is NOT true about Renshaw cells:
questions.explanation: Renshaw cells ACTIVATE nearby alpha motor neurons - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Renshaw cells are inhibitory interneurons that provide recurrent inhibition of alpha motor neurons, preventing overexcitation. Options A, B, D, E are correct: lateral inhibition, recurrent inhibition, glycinergic, excited by cholinergic collaterals.
questions.keyConcept: Renshaw cells provide recurrent inhibition via glycine to prevent alpha motor neuron overexcitation.
options: Involved in lateral inhibition for sharpening of signals.
Involved in recurrent inhibition to prevent overexcitation in spinal cord.
A glycinergic neuron mediates its action.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The stretch reflex:
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is the fastest body reflex. Option B is correct. It is a monosynaptic reflex with minimal central delay (0.5-0.8 ms). Options A, C, D, E are incorrect: it is monosynaptic (not polysynaptic), receptor is muscle spindle (not Pacinian), has short (not long) central delay, results in contraction (not relaxation).
questions.keyConcept: The monosynaptic stretch reflex has the fastest conduction due to its simple, direct excitatory circuit.
options: Results in relaxation of the stretched muscle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the muscle spindle, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Intrafusal fibers are NOT excited during overstretch - this is NOT true. Option C is INCORRECT. Overstretch actually stimulates the muscle spindle, exciting intrafusal fibers. Options A, B, D, E are correct: primary afferent responds to static length and rate, extrafusal stretch does stretch intrafusal, spindles are parallel to extrafusal, two fiber types exist.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles detect stretch; overstretch excites intrafusal fibers, increasing Ia afferent discharge.
options: The primary afferent fibers responds to the static length of muscle as well as to its rate of change in length.
Stretching the extrafusal fibres causes the intrafusal muscle fibres to be stretched.
They are excited during overstretch of the muscle.
They are parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Consists of two types of intrafusal fibers

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Regarding the stretch reflex, which sentence is NOT true:
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is a polysynaptic reflex - NOT TRUE. Option C is INCORRECT. Stretch reflex is MONOsynaptic (one synapse between Ia afferent and alpha motor neuron). Options A, B, D, E are correct: elicited by passive stretch, depends on spindle parallel to extrafusal, causes muscle contraction, inhibits antagonists.
questions.keyConcept: The stretch reflex is the prototypical monosynaptic reflex with a single excitatory synapse.
options: Can be elicited by passive stretch.
Depends on the muscle spindle which is a mechanoreceptor present parallel to the extrafusal muscle fibers.
Stretch of a muscle is followed by its contraction.
Is associated with simultaneous inhibition of the antagonist muscle.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The gamma efferent system:
questions.explanation: Gamma efferent system controls spindle sensitivity during voluntary movements. Option A is correct. Gamma motor neurons adjust spindle sensitivity so it remains responsive during muscle contraction when extrafusal fibers shorten. Options B, C, D, E are incorrect: gamma supplies all intrafusal zones, vestibulospinal facilitates (not inhibits) gamma, stimulation causes more (not less) spindle discharge, gamma does not contract extrafusal fibers.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neurons maintain muscle spindle sensitivity during movement by contracting intrafusal fibers.
options: Controls spindle sensitivity during voluntary movements.
Supplies the central zone of intrafusal muscle fibers.
Is inhibited by the vestibulo-spinal tract.
When stimulated, causes less discharge of central part of muscle spindles.
Produces direct contraction of extrafusal fibers.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The muscle spindles when stimulated transmit information about
questions.explanation: This question requires an essay-style answer about muscle spindle function. The muscle spindle is a specialized sensory organ that detects changes in muscle length and the rate of change. It consists of intrafusal fibers (nuclear bag and chain fibers) innervated by sensory (Ia and II) and motor (gamma) neurons. When stimulated, muscle spindles transmit information about: (1) Muscle length via static firing of primary endings, (2) Rate of length change via dynamic sensitivity of primary endings, (3) Muscle stretch velocity through Ia afferents, (4) Position sense through group II afferents. This information is crucial for proprioception, reflex coordination, and motor control. The gamma loop allows spindle sensitivity to be adjusted during voluntary movement so feedback remains accurate even as muscles contract.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindles provide proprioceptive feedback about muscle length and rate of change through Ia and II afferents, essential for motor coordination.
questions.modelAnswer:
When muscle spindles are stimulated, they transmit information about:

1. **Muscle Length**: The nuclear bag fibers detect static muscle length through sustained firing of primary (Ia) afferents and secondary (group II) afferents. This provides information about the position of the limb in space.

2. **Rate of Change in Length (Velocity)**: The nuclear chain fibers and dynamic sensitivity of primary endings respond to the speed of stretch. This is critical for detecting rapid movements and triggering protective reflexes.

3. **Velocity of Stretch**: Primary Ia afferents fire proportionally to how quickly a muscle is stretched, transmitting this information to the spinal cord and brain for real-time movement correction.

4. **Proprioceptive Position Sense**: Group II afferents provide static position information, contributing to kinesthesia and conscious awareness of limb position.

5. **Integration with Gamma Motor System**: Gamma efferent fibers adjust intrafusal fiber tension, maintaining spindle sensitivity during muscle contraction when extrafusal fibers shorten.

Clinical Significance: Muscle spindle dysfunction leads to impaired proprioception, ataxia, and poor motor coordination. The stretch reflex arc (muscle spindle → Ia afferent → spinal cord → alpha motor neuron → muscle contraction) is the fastest reflex pathway in the body, essential for posture and movement stability.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists
questions.explanation: Insomnia is NOT an adverse effect of direct D2 receptor agonists. Option C is correct. D2 agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) commonly cause hallucinations, dyskinesia (especially with long-term use), and impulse control disorders. Insomnia is not a typical adverse effect; actually, these drugs can cause daytime sleepiness. Amantadine is known to cause insomnia.
questions.keyConcept: D2 agonists cause neuropsychiatric effects (hallucinations, dyskinesia, impulse control disorders) but not insomnia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of amantadine
questions.explanation: Daytime sleepiness is NOT an adverse effect of amantadine. Option B is correct. Amantadine causes hallucinations, livedo reticularis (skin rash), ankle edema, and tolerance. Insomnia is actually a known amantadine effect (along with dizziness). Daytime sleepiness is more typical of dopamine agonists.
questions.keyConcept: Amantadine commonly causes insomnia, livedo reticularis, and ankle edema, but not daytime sleepiness.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following antiparkinsonian drug (s) induce (s) Insomnia
questions.explanation: Selegiline and Amantadine induce insomnia. Option D is correct. Both selegiline (MAO-B inhibitor) and amantadine (dopamine release enhancer) can cause insomnia as an adverse effect. L-dopa can also cause insomnia but the question specifically asks about drugs that induce insomnia.
questions.keyConcept: MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline) and amantadine are antiparkinsonian drugs that can cause insomnia as an adverse effect.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug can be used alone in treatment of Parkinson disease
questions.explanation: Pramipexole can be used alone in treatment of Parkinson disease. Option B is correct. Pramipexole is a D2/D3 dopamine agonist that can be used as monotherapy in early Parkinson's disease. L-dopa is combined with carbidopa/benserazide (not used alone). Entacapone is a COMT inhibitor added to L-dopa. Carbidopa is a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor that cannot penetrate BBB.
questions.keyConcept: D2 agonists like pramipexole can be used as monotherapy in early Parkinson's disease due to their ability to directly stimulate dopamine receptors.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drugs can minimize motor complication of using l-dopa in advanced Parkinson’s disease except
questions.explanation: Pyridoxine does NOT minimize motor complications of L-dopa. Option E is correct. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) actually interferes with L-dopa efficacy by enhancing peripheral decarboxylation. MAO-B inhibitors, COMT inhibitors, amantadine, and D2 agonists all help reduce motor complications (on-off phenomenon, dyskinesia).
questions.keyConcept: Pyridoxine (B6) interferes with L-dopa metabolism and should be avoided in Parkinsonism treatment.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Addition of the following drugs to L dopa produce all the following except
questions.explanation: Entacapone DECREASES L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Entacapone inhibits COMT, which DECREASES L-dopa metabolism, thereby INCREASING its bioavailability and duration of action. Domperidone decreases nausea (A is correct). Benztropine decreases absorption (B is correct). Apomorphine decreases off time (C is correct).
questions.keyConcept: COMT inhibitors like entacapone prolong L-dopa action by preventing its peripheral breakdown.
options: Domperidone / decreases l dopa induced nausea & vomiting
Apomorphine / decreases off time of on-off phenomena
Entacapone / Decrease L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about antiparkinsonian drugs
questions.explanation: Apomorphine is NOT taken orally - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Apomorphine is a D1/D2 agonist given by subcutaneous injection (not orally) for acute akinetic episodes in advanced Parkinson's. Selegiline is MAO-B inhibitor (correct). Entacapone is COMT inhibitor (correct). Amantadine increases dopamine release (correct).
questions.keyConcept: Apomorphine requires subcutaneous injection due to poor oral bioavailability and is used for acute rescue in advanced Parkinson's.
options: Selegiline is selective MAO-B inhibitor and decreases end of dose akinesia induced by L-dopa
Entacapone is selective COMT inhibitor and decreases of time of on/off effect of L dopa.
Amantadine increases dopamine release & blocks Glutamate (NMDA) receptors
Apomorphine taken orally to decrease off time & sudden akinetic episodes in advanced Parkinson’s disease

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is a wrong statement about therapy of Parkinson’s disease
questions.explanation: Vitamin B6 is NOT recommended - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Pyridoxine (B6) enhances peripheral decarboxylation of L-dopa, reducing its CNS availability. High protein diet reduces L-dopa absorption (correct). Fiber-rich diet helps constipation (correct). Beta-blockers can help tremors (correct).
questions.keyConcept: Pyridoxine (B6) should be avoided in patients taking L-dopa as it accelerates peripheral metabolism of the drug.
options: High protein diet is not recommended in the same time with L- dopa administration
Multivitamin including vitamin B6 is recommended to improve general condition of the patient
Diet rich in fibers is useful to minimize constipation especially if the patient on Benztropine therapy.
A Beta blocker may be added in the therapy to control tremors

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Cross match
questions.explanation: This matching question requires pairing drug names with their adverse effects. Amantadine causes insomnia, livedo reticularis, and ankle edema. Entacapone causes orange discoloration of urine and diarrhea. Bromocriptine causes vasospasm and cardiac fibrosis. Selegiline causes insomnia and hallucination. Pramipexole causes daytime sleepiness and impulse control disorders. Benztropine causes dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention (anticholinergic effects).
questions.keyConcept: Antiparkinsonian drugs have distinct adverse effect profiles important for clinical management and drug selection.

pairs.target: Day time sleepiness & impulse control disorders

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Addition of carbidopa to L dopa increases risk of all the following adverse effects except
questions.explanation: Nausea & vomiting is NOT increased by adding carbidopa. Option C is correct. Carbidopa prevents peripheral conversion of L-dopa to dopamine, reducing peripheral side effects including nausea/vomiting. However, it increases brain dopamine, which can increase CNS adverse effects: dyskinesia, hallucinations, and confusion.
questions.keyConcept: Carbidopa reduces peripheral L-dopa side effects (nausea) but increases central dopaminergic effects (dyskinesia, hallucinations).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Conscious sedation may be induced by
questions.explanation: Fentanyl with Midazolam induces conscious sedation. Option A is correct. This combination (opioid + benzodiazepine) provides analgesia and amnesia for conscious sedation in minor procedures. Droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia (B). Domperidone is antiemetic (C).
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation combines fentanyl (analgesia) with midazolam (anxiolysis/amnesia) for procedural sedation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not correctly matched to its use:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is not used for panic attack - this is NOT correctly matched. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is used for generalized anxiety, not panic attacks (which require benzodiazepines or SSRIs). Diazepam for muscle spasticity (A correct). Midazolam for anesthesia (B correct). Clonazepam for epilepsy (C correct).
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a selective anxiolytic for generalized anxiety but lacks efficacy for panic attacks.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following concerning zolpidem is not true
questions.explanation: Zolpidem is LESS liable to induce rebound insomnia than benzodiazepines - this is NOT true. Option C is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has more rebound insomnia potential compared to benzodiazepines because of its short half-life and selective BZ1 receptor action. Options A, B, D are true: zolpidem is short-acting with less hangover, acts on BZ1 receptor, and has less tolerance/dependence than BZDs.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has a short half-life and less hangover than benzodiazepines, but can cause rebound insomnia due to its short duration of action.
options: It is a short acting hypnotic causing less hang over than benzodiazepines
More liable to induce rebound insomnia & disturbance in REM sleep than benzodiazepines.
Its use is associated with less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The major limitation to the use of benzodiazepines in anxiety is:
questions.explanation: Dependence is the major limitation to benzodiazepine use. Option C is correct. Benzodiazepines cause physical and psychological dependence with chronic use, limiting their long-term use. Options A, B, D are less accurate: flumazenil is an antidote (A is wrong), cardiovascular depression is rare (B), and respiratory depression is mainly with high doses or combined with other depressants (D).
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dependence is the primary clinical limitation, requiring careful prescribing and monitoring.
options: No antidote is available if overdose toxicity occurs.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is preferred for treatment of anxiety with panic attacks:
questions.explanation: Alprazolam is preferred for panic attacks. Option B is correct. Alprazolam is a high-potency benzodiazepine with rapid onset, effective for acute panic attacks. Buspirone has delayed onset (weeks) (A). Haloperidol is an antipsychotic (C). Zolpidem is a hypnotic (D).
questions.keyConcept: High-potency benzodiazepines like alprazolam are first-line for acute panic attacks due to rapid onset.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: An anxiolytic useful in a patient with a history of drug dependence is:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is preferred in patients with drug dependence history. Option A is correct. Buspirone has no abuse potential, no physical dependence, and can be used safely in patients with history of substance abuse. All other benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, lorazepam) have dependence liability.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's lack of dependence makes it safe for patients with substance abuse history.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The dose of benzodiazepines should be adjusted in:
questions.explanation: Dose adjustment is needed in elderly AND with alcohol AND with hepatic dysfunction. Option D is correct. All three factors require dose adjustment: elderly have reduced metabolism, alcohol potentiates CNS depression, hepatic dysfunction impairs metabolism of benzodiazepines.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine dosing requires adjustment in elderly, hepatic impairment, and when combined with CNS depressants.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following concerning the use of benzodiazepines is not true
questions.explanation: Shorter acting agents are NOT preferred as anxiolytics - this is NOT true. Option D is incorrect. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, clonazepam) are preferred for anxiety because they provide steady plasma levels. Short-acting agents (triazolam) cause more rebound anxiety and are used for insomnia. Options A, B, C are correct: abuse causes memory loss, toxic dose causes prolonged sleep, flumazenil reverses respiratory depression.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines are preferred for anxiety due to stable plasma concentrations and reduced rebound effects.
options: Abuse is associated with memory loss.
Toxic dose results in prolonged sleep.
Respiratory depression is reversed by flumazenil.
Shorter acting agents are preferred as anxiolytics.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A drug whose toxic dose results in prolonged sleep reversed by flumazenil
questions.explanation: Triazolam toxic dose results in prolonged sleep reversed by flumazenil. Option C is correct. Triazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine; overdose causes prolonged sedation reversed by flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist). Pentobarbital and phenobarbital are barbiturates (not reversed by flumazenil). Buspirone is not a sedative.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine overdose but not barbiturate overdose.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Flumazenil is an antidote for all the following Except:
questions.explanation: Buspirone is NOT reversed by flumazenil. Option B is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine receptor antagonist. Triazolam (A), zolpidem (C), and diazepam (D) are all benzodiazepine-related drugs reversed by flumazenil. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A agonist anxiolytic that does not act on benzodiazepine receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil only reverses benzodiazepines and zolpidem; it does not reverse buspirone (5-HT1A agonist) or barbiturates.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: All the following characteristics are shared by flumazenil and naloxone Except:
questions.explanation: Flumazenil and naloxone are NOT given orally - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Both flumazenil and naloxone are given parenterally (IV), not orally, because they have poor oral bioavailability and rapid first-pass metabolism. Options A, C, D are correct shared characteristics.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil and naloxone require parenteral administration due to poor oral bioavailability and rapid hepatic metabolism.
options: Have shorter t1/2 than their respective agonists.
Given in anesthesia to reverse CNS depression of their agonists.
Specific respiratory stimulants in benzodiazepine or opioid toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Abuse potential of buspirone is low because
questions.explanation: Buspirone has delayed onset of action - this explains low abuse potential. Option C is correct. Unlike benzodiazepines which act immediately, buspirone takes 2-4 weeks for anxiolytic effect. This delayed onset, combined with lack of sedation and no GABA activity, results in low abuse potential.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's delayed onset of action contributes to its minimal abuse potential compared to benzodiazepines.
options: It has a weak anxiolytic effect
It has no recognizable effect on brain neurotransmitters.
It has a delayed onset of action.
Its marked sedating effect is troublesome.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following anxiolytic drug do not act through GABA
questions.explanation: Buspirone does not act through GABA. Option B is correct. Buspirone is a 5-HT1A partial agonist anxiolytic. Zolpidem (A), lorazepam (C), and phenobarbital (D) all enhance GABAergic transmission. Buspirone works through serotonin modulation.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone is a 5-HT1A serotonin receptor partial agonist, distinct from GABA-acting anxiolytics.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug has no sedative hypnotic effect
questions.explanation: Flumazenil has no sedative hypnotic effect. Option C is correct. Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist that blocks GABA-benzodiazepine receptors. It reverses sedation and would not cause sedation. Antihistamines (A), tricyclics (B), and clonidine (D) all have sedative effects.
questions.keyConcept: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist with no intrinsic sedative activity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following drug is not matched with its mechanism of action
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5HT1A AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is a selective 5-HT1A partial agonist (not antagonist). Options A, B, C are correct: diazepam increases frequency of chloride channel opening, zolpidem binds BZ1 receptor, barbiturates increase duration of channel opening.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's anxiolytic effect comes from 5-HT1A receptor partial agonism, not antagonism.
options: Diazepam increases frequency of opening of chloride channels
Zolpidem binds with BZD1 subtype → increases GABA activity
Barbiturates increase duration of opening of chloride channels

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is a Wrong statement about Barbiturates
questions.explanation: Barbiturates are NOT strong enzyme inducers - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Barbiturates are potent CYP450 inducers, increasing metabolism of many drugs. Options A, C, D are correct: low therapeutic index, dose-dependent CNS depression, no specific antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Barbiturates are potent enzyme inducers that increase hepatic metabolism of many co-administered drugs.
options: Dose dependent CNS depression up to coma

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following statement is Wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of Benzodiazepines
questions.explanation: Clinical duration of long-acting BZDs is longer than actual half-life - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Long-acting BZDs form active metabolites that prolong their effect beyond the parent compound's half-life. Options A, B, D are correct: IM absorption is slower (except lorazepam), lorazepam uses glucuronidation not oxidation, lorazepam has no active metabolites.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines have prolonged effects due to active metabolites, making actual duration longer than parent half-life.
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BDZs is shorter than the actual half life as they form active metabolites

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: BDZs do not induce the following effect
questions.explanation: BDZs do NOT decrease stage II NREM sleep. Option B is correct. Benzodiazepines decrease REM sleep and stages III/IV (deep sleep), but actually increase stage II NREM sleep (light sleep). This is why they suppress deep sleep and REM sleep while promoting light sleep.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepines suppress REM and deep sleep (III/IV) while preserving or increasing light sleep (stage II).
options: Decrease stage II of NREM sleep
Decrease stage III & IV of NREM sleep

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is not an adverse effect of BZDS
questions.explanation: Decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal is NOT an adverse effect - it is a withdrawal effect. Option B is incorrect. Insomnia and REM rebound occur on withdrawal, not as direct adverse effects during use. Options A, C, D are correct direct adverse effects: sedation/hangover, cognitive impairment, tolerance/dependence.
questions.keyConcept: Benzodiazepine withdrawal causes REM rebound insomnia; direct adverse effects include sedation, cognitive impairment, and dependence.
options: Insomnia & decrease in REM sleep on sudden withdrawal
Decrease in cognitive function of the brain

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The following is a Wrong statement about BZDs
