This enzyme normally catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs): (1) Leucine -> acetoacetate. (2) Isoleucine -> acetoacetate + acetyl-CoA. (3) Valine -> propionyl-CoA. In MSUD, BCKDH deficiency causes accumulation of BCAAs and their corresponding alpha-keto acids in blood, urine, and tissues. Clinical features: Characteristic maple syrup odor of urine, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, neurological deterioration, seizures, developmental delay, coma and death if untreated. Management: Dietary restriction of BCAAs, thiamine supplementation (if variant form), and liver transplantation in classic severe forms.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention the name of three biochemical reactions need vitamin B1.
questions.explanation: Vitamin B1 (thiamine) is required as thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) by three key biochemical reactions: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin B1 (as TPP) is essential for pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.modelAnswer: Three biochemical reactions requiring vitamin B1 (as thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP): (1) Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex - converts pyruvate -> acetyl-CoA (link reaction between glycolysis and the citric acid cycle). Requires TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, and FAD/NAD+. Deficiency blocks entry of pyruvate into the CAC, shunting pyruvate to lactate (lactic acidosis in B1 deficiency). (2) Alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex - converts alpha-ketoglutarate -> succinyl-CoA in the CAC. Similar cofactor requirements to pyruvate dehydrogenase. Important for nitrogen metabolism via glutamate. (3) Transketolase - in the pentose phosphate pathway (non-oxidative phase). Catalyzes transfer of a 2-carbon unit between sugar phosphates. Transketolase activity in erythrocytes is used as a functional test for thiamine status (low activity indicates B1 deficiency).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention two Biochemical tests of thiamine status
questions.explanation: Two biochemical tests for thiamine status are the erythrocyte transketolase activity assay and urinary thiamine excretion measurement.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine status is assessed by erythrocyte transketolase activity and urinary thiamine/TPP excretion.
questions.modelAnswer: Two biochemical tests of thiamine status: (1) Erythrocyte transketolase activity (ETKA) - functional assay. Thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) is an essential cofactor for transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway. In thiamine deficiency, erythrocyte transketolase activity is reduced. The test measures enzyme activity with and without added TPP in vitro. The TPP effect (percentage increase in activity when TPP is added) indicates the degree of deficiency: less than 15% = normal; 15-25% = marginal deficiency; greater than 25% = significant deficiency. This is the most sensitive functional test for B1 deficiency. (2) Urinary thiamine excretion - reflects recent dietary intake. Low urinary thiamine (less than 100 micrograms/24h) indicates deficiency. However, this reflects acute intake rather than tissue stores. Less reliable than transketolase assay because it fluctuates with recent dietary intake. Additional test: Blood thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) level via HPLC - direct but expensive.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Illustrate the biochemical reaction of pyruvate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, requiring five cofactors: thiamine TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+.
questions.keyConcept: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is a multi-enzyme complex requiring TPP, lipoic acid, CoA, FAD, and NAD+ to convert pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
questions.modelAnswer: Biochemical reaction of pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH complex): Pyruvate + NAD+ + CoA-SH + TPP + lipoic acid -> Acetyl-CoA + NADH + H+ + CO2. Location: Mitochondrial matrix. The PDH complex consists of three enzymatic components: (1) Pyruvate decarboxylase (E1) - requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP); decarboxylates pyruvate to hydroxyethyl-TPP. (2) Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase (E2) - requires lipoic acid (covalently attached); transfers the acetyl group to CoA, generating acetyl-CoA and leaving reduced lipoic acid. (3) Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase (E3) - requires FAD (from riboflavin) and NAD+ (from niacin); reoxidizes reduced lipoic acid back to its oxidized form, producing NADH. Regulation: Product inhibition by NADH and acetyl-CoA. Covalent regulation by PDH kinase (inhibits via phosphorylation) and PDH phosphatase (activates via dephosphorylation). Allosteric activation by pyruvate and ADP. Clinical significance: Thiamine deficiency (beriberi) causes accumulation of pyruvate and lactic acidosis due to impaired PDH function.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention the name of two diseases from thiamine deficiency.
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (CNS) and wet beriberi (cardiovascular) as the two major disease manifestations.
questions.keyConcept: Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (CNS) and wet beriberi (cardiovascular disease) primarily.
questions.modelAnswer: Two diseases from thiamine deficiency: (1) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome - CNS manifestation of thiamine deficiency. Wernicke encephalopathy (acute): Classic triad - ophthalmoplegia (or nystagmus), ataxia, and confusion. Due to impaired glucose metabolism in brainstem and thalamic nuclei (mammillary bodies). Can progress to Korsakoff syndrome (chronic) - anterograde and retrograde amnesia, confabulation, personality changes. Most common in chronic alcoholics. (2) Wet beriberi - cardiovascular manifestation. High-output cardiac failure with peripheral vasodilation causing cardiomegaly, tachycardia, peripheral edema, and warm extremities. Due to impaired ATP production in cardiac muscle. Can rapidly progress to heart failure. (3) Dry beriberi - peripheral neuropathy with sensory and motor deficits (purely neurological, no cardiac involvement). All forms respond to thiamine replacement.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention three causes and three symptoms of pellagra “niacin deficiency”
questions.explanation: Pellagra (niacin/vitamin B3 deficiency) results from dietary deficiency or conditions impairing tryptophan-to-niacin conversion; it presents with dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
questions.keyConcept: Pellagra results from niacin deficiency and presents with the 3 Ds: dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia.
questions.modelAnswer: Three causes of pellagra: (1) Dietary deficiency - inadequate intake of niacin and tryptophan. Common in populations relying heavily on corn (maize), as niacin in corn is bound and poorly bioavailable. (2) Malabsorption - conditions causing fat malabsorption reduce absorption of niacin and tryptophan. (3) Carcinoid syndrome - tumor diverts tryptophan away from niacin synthesis toward serotonin production, causing functional niacin deficiency. Hartnup disease is a genetic condition impairing tryptophan absorption. Other causes: chronic alcoholism, isoniazid therapy. Three symptoms: (1) Dermatitis - photosensitive dermatitis, particularly on sun-exposed areas (Casals necklace around the neck, or affecting hands and feet), with pigmented rash. (2) Diarrhea - inflammatory diarrhea due to mucosal atrophy. (3) Dementia - confusion, disorientation, and cognitive decline progressing to frank psychosis and death if untreated (the 4th D = death without treatment).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Give a short account on two folate analogues “antagonists”.
questions.explanation: Two folate analogues are methotrexate and trimethoprim, which inhibit dihydrofolate reductase and thereby block purine and thymidylate synthesis.
questions.keyConcept: Methotrexate and trimethoprim are folate antagonists inhibiting DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Two folate analogues (antagonists): (1) Methotrexate - a structural analogue of folic acid. It competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking conversion of dihydrofolate (DHF) to tetrahydrofolate (THF). This depletes all folate cofactors needed for: purine synthesis (via 10-formyl THF), thymidylate synthesis (via 5,10-methylene THF), and amino acid interconversions. Result: Impaired DNA and RNA synthesis, particularly affecting rapidly dividing cells. Used in: cancer chemotherapy (high dose), autoimmune diseases (low dose), ectopic pregnancy. Toxicity: myelosuppression, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, teratogenicity. Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues from toxicity. (2) Trimethoprim - a folate antagonist that selectively inhibits bacterial DHFR (50,000x more potent against bacterial than human DHFR). Used in combination with sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) for UTI, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, and other infections.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention two different sources and two fates of methylene.
questions.explanation: Methylene (CH2) groups are derived from serine and glycine catabolism, and are consumed primarily in thymidylate synthesis and the methionine synthase reaction.
questions.keyConcept: Methylene (CH2) is derived from serine/glycine and is consumed primarily in dTMP synthesis and the folate cycle.
questions.modelAnswer: Two different sources of methylene (CH2): (1) Serine - the primary source. Serine hydroxymethyltransferase (SHMT) catalyzes: Serine + THF -> glycine + N5,N10-methylene THF. Serine provides the beta-carbon as the methylene group. This is the main source of one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis. (2) Glycine - also donates one-carbon units via its cleavage to CO2 + NH3 + N5,N10-methylene THF (by glycine cleavage enzyme system or SHMT in reverse). Two different fates of methylene: (1) Thymidylate synthesis - N5,N10-methylene THF donates both a methyl group and reducing power to convert dUMP -> dTMP (catalyzed by thymidylate synthase). This is the main fate of methylene THF and the basis of 5-fluorouracil chemotherapy. THF is oxidized to DHF in this reaction. (2) Methionine synthase reaction - methylene THF (as N5-methyl THF) donates its methyl group to homocysteine (via methionine synthase, requiring B12) to regenerate methionine. This is the only reaction that removes methylated THF from the folate pool.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Mention two different sources of methenyl and formyl.
questions.explanation: Methenyl and formyl groups in one-carbon metabolism are derived from serine catabolism and from the catabolism of tryptophan and histidine.
questions.keyConcept: Methenyl and formyl groups derive from serine, tryptophan, and histidine catabolism, feeding into purine and formyl-Met-tRNA synthesis.
questions.modelAnswer: Two different sources of methenyl: (1) Serine catabolism - N5,N10-methylene THF (from serine via SHMT) can be oxidized to N5,N10-methenyl THF by serine hydroxymethyltransferase in reverse or by methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase (MTHFD). Methenyl THF is an intermediate in the conversion of formyl groups to methylene groups and vice versa. (2) Tryptophan catabolism - the kynurenine pathway produces N-formylkynurenine, which generates one-carbon units at the formyl and methenyl oxidation levels. Two different sources of formyl: (1) Histidine catabolism - the catabolism of L-histidine produces N-formimino glutamate, which transfers a formyl group to THF (generating N10-formyl THF) via the formiminotransferase reaction. (2) Purine ring biosynthesis - N10-formyl THF provides two separate formyl groups for the synthesis of the purine ring (at positions C2 and C8 of the purine nucleus). These formyl groups are transferred by transformylases (GAR transformylase and AICAR transformylase) during de novo purine synthesis. Additionally, mitochondrial protein synthesis requires formyl-methionine (fMet) for the initiator tRNA.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) influx through voltage-gated channels drives the rapid upstroke of the neuronal action potential. When threshold is reached, Nav1.5/1.2 channels open, causing rapid depolarization from -70 mV toward +30 mV.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium ion influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels is responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The resting membrane potential is closest to the equilibrium potential of which ion?
questions.explanation: The resting membrane potential (approximately -70 mV in neurons) closely matches the equilibrium potential of K+ (approximately -90 mV) because the membrane at rest is most permeable to K+ via leak channels.
questions.keyConcept: The resting membrane potential approximates the K+ equilibrium potential due to high resting K+ permeability.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A teenager girl discovered loss of sensation of her right hand and on examination the doctor discovered loss of pain and temperature of distal part of the upper limb. Also, there was diminished pain and temperature on left hand. The condition was diagnosed as cavitations of the spinal cord.
questions.explanation: The bilateral distal upper limb sensory loss (loss of pain and temperature) with crossed pattern indicates syringomyelia — a cavity in the central spinal cord that disrupts crossing spinothalamic fibers first.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia causes bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved proprioception due to selective destruction of crossing spinothalamic tract fibers in the central cord.

subQuestions.text: Why the pain and temperature fibers are only involved in this case?
Where is the most common site for such condition?

questions.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: Syringomyelia (cavitation of the spinal cord). Why pain and temperature fibers are only involved: The spinothalamic tract fibers (carrying pain and temperature) cross the spinal cord at the anterior white commissure, which is located centrally. The expanding syrinx (fluid‑filled cavity) disrupts these crossing fibers bilaterally at its level before affecting other tracts. Proprioception and motor function are preserved because the posterior columns (carrying proprioception) are located posteriorly and the corticospinal tracts are in the lateral columns — these are spared initially. Most common site: The cervical region is the most common site for syringomyelia, particularly at C6–C8 segments. This explains why symptoms typically begin in the upper limbs (cape‑like distribution) before spreading to the trunk and lower limbs as the syrinx expands.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A lady 55 years old, developed right sided hemiplegia mainly in the upper limb due to cerebrovascular accident as proved by MRI. The lesion affects the frontal and parietal lobes.
questions.explanation: The presentation of right-sided hemiplegia predominantly affecting the upper limb, with frontal and parietal lobe involvement on MRI, suggests a stroke in the territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), specifically the superior division.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb‑predominant hemiplegia with frontal/parietal involvement indicates MCA territory infarction affecting the motor cortex homunculus.

subQuestions.text: Which vessel is most likely affected?

questions.modelAnswer: Diagnosis: Cerebrovascular accident (ischemic stroke) in the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, specifically affecting the right hemisphere (left-sided body symptoms — wait, the question states right-sided hemiplegia with MRI showing frontal and parietal lobe lesions). The hemiplegia is mainly in the upper limb because the motor cortex representation of the upper limb (hand and arm) lies in the precentral gyrus supplied by the MCA. Which vessel is most likely affected: The middle cerebral artery (MCA). The MCA supplies the lateral surface of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes — including the primary motor cortex (precentral gyrus) and premotor area controlling the upper extremity. The upper limb representation is particularly affected because it occupies the largest area of the motor homunculus in the MCA territory. The fact that the lower limb is relatively spared (hemiplegia mainly in upper limb) is consistent with MCA rather than ACA territory infarction, as the lower limb motor area lies on the medial surface of the hemisphere (anterior cerebral artery territory).
